cues.text: Let us now turn to the application of everything we have said about DevOps, and we will do it through a case: the MIND CA application, looking at MTN's DevOps culture and metrics.
Begin with how the case describes the organisation.
MTN's teaching case describes cross-functional squads.
A squad is a small team that brings together the different skills needed to build and run a service, so that people do not have to hand work from one department to the next and wait.
These squads have service ownership.
That means each squad is responsible for a particular service, not only while it is being built, but also while it is running and being supported.
Alongside the squads, the case describes a platform team.
The platform team provides a standard delivery pipeline.
A delivery pipeline is the automated path that takes a change from a developer's work through building, testing and release.
By standardising it, the platform team means every squad does not have to invent its own route to production.
Now, what is DevOps itself?
DevOps is a cultural and operational practice.
Notice both words.
It is cultural, because it depends on how people think and behave, and it is operational, because it changes how work is actually done.
It combines four things: collaboration, automation, measurement and shared responsibility.
Collaboration means development and operations people work together instead of in separate silos.
Automation means repetitive steps such as testing and deployment are done by tools, which makes them faster and more consistent.
Measurement means we use data to see how delivery and service are really performing.
And shared responsibility means that when something goes wrong, it is owned jointly, not thrown over a wall to someone else.
A well-known way to remember these ideas is the acronym CALMS.
It stands for Culture, Automation, Lean, Measurement and Sharing.
Culture is the collaborative, shared-responsibility mindset.
Automation is the use of tooling to remove manual effort.
Lean is about reducing waste and queues.
Think of a queue as work sitting idle, waiting for approval or for another team, and waste as effort that adds no value for the customer.
Measurement is tracking how the system performs.
And Sharing is shared learning, which, as the source puts it, reduces repeated failures: if one team learns from an incident and shares it, other teams do not make the same mistake again.
Next, the outcomes that the case reports.
Please keep in mind that these are case-reported outcomes.
I will go through each one in order.
First, releases.
They moved from two to four per year to more than fifty per week.
Second, delivery lead time, which is the time from starting a change to having it delivered.
It moved from six to nine months to two to four weeks.
Third, recovery time, which is how long it takes to restore service after a failure.
It moved from four to eight hours to under thirty minutes.
Fourth, availability, meaning the proportion of time the service is working.
It moved from 99.0 percent to 99.95 percent.
Fifth, estimated compute-cost savings of around 30 percent.
Note the word estimated.
Now an important point about how to treat these numbers.
The source says these claims are case evidence.
They are what the case reports, not independently verified results, and we should present them that way.
There is also a caution about the release counts.
Deployment counts may compare different units.
Before, a release may have meant a release of one large monolith, a single big application deployed as a whole.
Afterwards, a deployment may mean an individual service being released on its own.
Those are not the same thing.
So, unless we have clear definitions of what is being counted, we should not calculate a precise like-for-like speedup from two to four per year against fifty per week.
The direction of change is meaningful, but a neat multiplication would claim more than the source supports.
Now the availability arithmetic, which we can do carefully.
Availability went from 99.0 percent to 99.95 percent.
The improvement is 99.95 minus 99.0, which is 0.95 percentage points.
Notice we say percentage points, because we are subtracting one percentage from another.
Next, consider the unavailable fraction, the part of the time the service is not working.
At 99.0 percent availability, the expected unavailable fraction is 1 percent.
At 99.95 percent, it is 0.05 percent.
The drop is from 1 percent to 0.05 percent.
Measured relative to the starting point, that is 0.95 divided by 1, which is a 95 percent relative decrease.
The source adds a qualification: this holds under comparable measurement, meaning availability must be measured the same way before and after for the comparison to be fair.
Finally, the lesson about balance.
Speed alone is not success.
The source says to track financial correctness, fraud, service reliability and customer experience alongside velocity.
Velocity means how fast we deliver.

For a company like MTN, which handles payments and large numbers of customers, shipping quickly is only valuable if money is still processed correctly, fraud is kept in check, services stay reliable, and customers have a good experience.
So a sound set of measures looks at all of these together, not at release frequency on its own.
